text.p: The dollar closed higher against the mark here, buoyed by comments from a senior U.S. Federal Reserve official saying that a majority of Fed banks submitted requests for a rise in the discount rate, traders said.

The unnamed source said eight of the 12 district banks in the Federal Reserve System requested a rise in the 5.0 percent discount rate and that three out of eight called for a 50 basis points increase.
Slightly higher-than-expected U.S. industrial production data and capacity utilisation figures for August also lent the dollar a helping hand for its climb higher, analysts said.
"It's a combination of dollar-positive elements that allowed the dollar to go higher, such as the Fed comments and the latest data," said Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered.
The source said requests for a discount rate rise came from banks in Fed districts with rapid growth and tight labour market conditions or that have a "hawkish", anti-inflation reputation.
The source also said the consensus is centered around a 25 basis points rise in the Fed funds rate, now at 5.25 percent.
Dealers said the comments caught the market off guard even though reports that regional Fed presidents have pushed for a rate hike have circulated for several weeks.
At 1452 GMT the dollar was at 1.5141/44 marks and 110.15/25 yen, compared with 1.5112/16 and 110.17/27 in late European trading on Monday.
Despite intraday gains of half a pfennig the dollar run into stiff resistance at 1.5160, a key technical level broken briefly last Friday but still in place as a major upside barrier.
"We need a convincing break of that level but it's difficult because there's an awful lot of offers in that area," said a trader at a U.S. bank.
The mark's extended weakness on the European crosses also boosted the dollar, the dealer said.

The French franc set a six-week high at 3.3966 per mark as dealers kept a close eye on the Franco-German summit in the Bavarian town of Kempten. Concern about the French budget, to be announced on Wednesday, has eased.
German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said France and Germany reaffirmed their commitment to keep up efforts to cut government spending in order to meet criteria for European currency union.

A much-awaited batch of U.S. economic data supported the dollar but failed to spark much excitement as analysts said they were not a "make-or-break" piece of information for Fed policy at the next FOMC meeting on September 24.
Industrial production rose 0.5 percent in August from the previous month compared with a 0.4 percent forecast. Capacity utilisation was at 83.5 percent against 83.3 percent expected.
